co_flood.text: Quiapo. 3 June 1998. 3:58 in the morning. The Pasig has climbed four streets inland, and it is still climbing.
Punerarya Dimaculangan, Hidalgo Street. The water is waist-deep in the viewing room. Two coffins float, and one of them is knocking from the inside.

co_flood.speaker: Kardo
co_flood.text: Mang Pido! I cut the line at the post. You've got no power, but you've got no fire either. That's the best I can do.

co_flood.speaker: Lolo Pido
co_flood.text: It's enough, Kardo. Get up the stairs. Take Ising and the baby to the roof.
On the landing, Ising holds a girl of three months against her shoulder. She does not move.

co_flood.speaker: Ising
co_flood.text: Pido. They're not knocking to get out. They're knocking to be let in.
Faces rise in the brown water. Not the dead from the coffins. Older dead. Drowned dead, from every flood this street has ever had, pulled up by something open below the city.

co_flood.speaker: Lolo Pido
co_flood.text: Then I'll send them home. Kardo, the stairs. Now.
Pido Dimaculangan, sundô of Quiapo, wraps a black panyo around his left wrist, draws the old sundang from under the counter, and steps down into the water.

co_rewind.text: The drowned break apart on the sundang and sink. For every one that sinks, two more rise. The water reaches Pido's chest.

co_rewind.speaker: Kardo
co_rewind.text: There's no end to them! Mang Pido, come up, there's no end!

co_rewind.speaker: Lolo Pido
co_rewind.text: There's an end. It's just not mine to spend.
He takes a pocket watch from his shirt. Balete-wood case, no maker's mark. He opens it, and turns the crown backward.
The hands run backward. So does the river.
The water slides off the walls. It pours down the stairs it came up, out the door it came in by, back along Hidalgo Street toward the river, like a sheet pulled off a bed.
Kardo counts out loud, because someone should. He counts to two hundred and fifty-seven. Four minutes and seventeen seconds.
When it is over, the parlor is dry. The coffins sit where they should. And the man holding the watch is ten years older than the man who opened it.

co_rewind.speaker: Teo
co_rewind.text: Kardo is staring at the watch.

co_rewind.speaker: Lolo Pido
co_rewind.text: Ten years. It always costs years. The watch keeps the account.

co_rewind.speaker: Lolo Pido
co_rewind.text: Ours. The family's. Every second we borrow, someone in this house pays back.

co_downriver.text: Two kilometres downriver, in Santa Ana, the water that left Quiapo arrives all at once.
A wall of it. Brown, fast, carrying a jeepney roof and a church pew. It takes the riverside houses in a single breath.
On one roof that holds, a boy of seventeen in a school uniform is screaming into the dark.
The ID card on his lanyard spins in the wind. VILLACORTA, GREGORIO. Fourth Year, Santa Ana High.
Back in Quiapo, at dawn, the stopped clocks on the parlor wall all read 4:17. Nobody winds them again.
And at the door, before the sun is fully up, someone knocks. Ising holds the baby a little closer, and does not answer it.

lamay_open.text: Quiapo. Today. Hidalgo Street, the second night of a wake.
Punerarya Dimaculangan's neon sign has two dead letters, so it reads PUNE  RYA DIMACU ANGAN. It has read that way since Teo was in grade school.
Inside: monobloc chairs, a coffee urn, a card table where the relatives play tong-its for the funeral fund, and a white coffin under the photo of a man in a jeepney driver's cap.

lamay_open.speaker: Teo
lamay_open.text: Ernesto Calma. Mang Berto. Fifty-eight. Drowned on España Boulevard on a night when it did not rain.

lamay_open.speaker: Teo
lamay_open.text: Twenty-two chairs. Fourteen cups. One urn, half full. Lola will ask me the numbers, so I count the numbers.
And at the head of the coffin, reading the ribbons on his own flowers, stands Mang Berto.

lamay_open.speaker: Teo
lamay_open.text: Don't look. Don't look. It's the second night. They always stand around on the second night.
The dead man turns his head. He has seen Teo see him.

lamay_open.speaker: Teo
lamay_open.text: Mang Berto is looking straight at me.
Teo nods. The dead man's eyebrows go up, and then, slowly, he nods back.

lamay_open.speaker: Teo
lamay_open.text: Fourteen years of pretending, and I just blew it on a jeepney driver.
Teo refills the urn. The dead man keeps watching him do it.

lamay_open.speaker: Teo
lamay_open.text: Fourteen years of pretending. I'm good at it. I'm very good at it.

debt_notice.text: At eleven, Kapitan Obet arrives in a pressed barong, with a sympathy envelope in one hand and a folder in the other.

debt_notice.speaker: Kapitan Obet
debt_notice.text: Condolence, condolence. Aling Nena, my deepest. Teo, iho. Where's your Lola?

debt_notice.speaker: Teo
debt_notice.text: Upstairs, Kap. It's a wake. Can it wait?

debt_notice.speaker: Kapitan Obet
debt_notice.text: Everything waits, iho. That's what interest is.
The folder. The 5-6 loan Lola took to keep the doors open, with the building as collateral. One hundred eighty thousand pesos, after interest. Due Friday.

debt_notice.speaker: Kapitan Obet
debt_notice.text: I'm not a monster. I have a buyer for you. Hiraya Energy, the green power people. They're buying old lots in Quiapo for cash. Your Lola pays me, keeps something, retires to the province. Everyone is happy.

debt_notice.speaker: Teo
debt_notice.text: Everyone but the people who need a funeral they can pay for in March.

debt_notice.speaker: Lola Ising
debt_notice.text: Obet. You'll have a coffee, and you'll put that folder away in front of Nena.
Lola Ising has come down the stairs without a sound. Seventy-five, small, in a housedress and a cardigan. Kapitan Obet puts the folder away.

debt_notice.speaker: Teo
debt_notice.text: Kap is still smiling at me.

remember.what: you threw him out of a wake

debt_notice.speaker: Kapitan Obet
debt_notice.text: ...The young. So much feeling. Friday, Ising.
He leaves. Two of the tong-its players clap, very quietly.
Teo pours. Lola touches his elbow on her way past, which is as close as she comes to saying thank you.
Kapitan Obet drinks his coffee standing, the way people do when they want you to know they have somewhere better to be.

hub_nena.text: Aling Nena sits nearest the coffin, rosary looped twice around her wrist.

hub_nena.speaker: Aling Nena
hub_nena.text: He came home that night soaked to the skin, Teo. Soaked. I said, it isn't raining, Berto. He said, I know.

hub_nena.speaker: Teo
hub_nena.text: Did he say where he'd been?

hub_nena.speaker: Aling Nena
hub_nena.text: The underpass by Evangelista. A child was crying in the water, he said, so he stopped the jeep. He went down to look. The water was warm, he said. Like a bath.

hub_nena.speaker: Aling Nena
hub_nena.text: Two days later they found him on España. Dry street. Lungs full of river.

hub_nena.speaker: Teo
hub_nena.text: A child crying in the water. Warm water. I know what Lola would say about that, and I know she'd say it quietly.
Over Aling Nena's shoulder, Mang Berto has stopped reading his ribbons. He is listening to his wife.

hub_coffin.text: Teo straightens the flowers, which is the only excuse anyone needs to stand by a coffin.

Mang Berto's mouth is sewn and waxed, Kardo's careful work. But a thin line of brown water has crept from the corner of his lips onto the white satin. It should not be there. Kardo does not make that kind of mistake.

hub_coffin.speaker: Teo
hub_coffin.text: Two days embalmed and he's still leaking river.
Teo touches the stain. It is warm, and it smells of rust, the way the Pasig smells where the old factories used to empty into it.
Across the coffin, the dead man looks down at the stain on his own pillow, and then at Teo, as if to say: you see it too.

hub_domeng.text: Mang Domeng sells candles outside Quiapo Church by day and sits at every wake on Hidalgo Street by night, for the coffee.

hub_domeng.speaker: Mang Domeng
hub_domeng.text: Teo. Sit. You look like a man who's counted the chairs twice.

hub_domeng.speaker: Mang Domeng
hub_domeng.text: Your Lola came to my stall on Tuesday. Paid for forty days of candles. In advance.

hub_domeng.speaker: Mang Domeng
hub_domeng.text: A pasiyam, then a forty-day. That's what you buy for the dead, iho. I asked her who for. She said, someone who won't be here to buy them.

hub_domeng.speaker: Teo
hub_domeng.text: Nobody in this house is dying. Nobody I know about.

hub_domeng.speaker: Mang Domeng
hub_domeng.text: I'm an old man and I sell wax. Don't listen to me. But listen to her, while she's talking.

hub_cards.text: At the card table, Berto's son Jun-jun is losing at tong-its and arguing with his uncle about who gets the jeepney franchise.

hub_cards.speaker: Jun-jun
hub_cards.text: He's not even buried and you want the route? Tito, I drove that route with him since I was fifteen!

hub_cards.speaker: Teo
hub_cards.text: Two more minutes and somebody throws a chair.

options: Deal yourself in and change the subject
Tell them Mang Berto can hear them

hub_cards.speaker: Teo
hub_cards.text: Deal me in. Twenty pesos. And tell me about his last fare, Jun-jun. Was it a good one?

hub_cards.speaker: Teo
hub_cards.text: He's right there. He can hear every word. Do you want that to be the last thing he hears?
Nobody laughs. At a wake on Hidalgo Street, nobody laughs at that.

hub_cards.speaker: Jun-jun
hub_cards.text: ...His last fare was weird. A man in a Hiraya Energy jacket. Paid in new bills, wanted the underpass by Evangelista, at midnight. Tatay said he smelled like a hospital.

hub_cards.speaker: Teo
hub_cards.text: Hiraya. Kapitan Obet's buyer. Twice in one night.

berto_ghost.text: Past midnight. The tong-its game breaks up. Aling Nena sleeps in her chair. The neon outside buzzes like a fly against glass.
Mang Berto sits down in the empty chair next to Teo.

berto_ghost.speaker: Mang Berto
berto_ghost.text: You nodded. You're Pido's grandson, the one who sees. He saw me too, iho, at my own father's wake, forty years ago. He nodded just like that.

berto_ghost.speaker: Mang Berto
berto_ghost.text: Iho. You can stop pretending. Your Lolo saw me at my father's wake, forty years ago. You have his face when you pretend.

berto_ghost.speaker: Teo
berto_ghost.text: ...You're supposed to go, Mang Berto. On the ninth night. That's how it works.

berto_ghost.speaker: Mang Berto
berto_ghost.text: And who tells Nena about the twelve thousand pesos in the jeepney seat cushion? The franchise fee. I was saving it. If I go, Jun-jun sells the jeep with the money inside it.

berto_ghost.speaker: Mang Berto
berto_ghost.text: There was a baby in the water. And then there wasn't a baby. There was something holding me under, and it was smiling.

berto_ghost.speaker: Mang Berto
berto_ghost.text: I still taste the river. Rust and rust and rust.
Water runs from his sleeves now, though he is sitting still. It pools on the tiles, brown and warm. His edges have begun to darken, like a photograph left in the sun.

berto_ghost.speaker: Teo
berto_ghost.text: Lola told me once, when I was small and she thought I wasn't listening: if they stay too long, they forget who they were. Then they only remember being hungry.

berto_ghost.speaker: Teo
berto_ghost.text: He's starting to forget. I can see it happen.

options: "I'll tell Nena about the cushion. I promise."
"It isn't my job, Mang Berto. I'm sorry."

berto_ghost.speaker: Mang Berto
berto_ghost.text: Twelve thousand. In the cushion. Tell her I wasn't drinking it.

berto_ghost.speaker: Teo
berto_ghost.text: I don't have an answer. Lola would. Lola always has an answer, and she never tells me.

lola_watch.text: Upstairs, Lola Ising is kneeling in front of the old aparador with a key Teo has never seen.
Half the room is in boxes. Clothes in sacks. A bus ticket on the bed, to Vigan, for tomorrow morning. One seat.

lola_watch.speaker: Teo
lola_watch.text: 'La. He's turning. Mang Berto. He's sitting downstairs and he's turning.

lola_watch.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_watch.text: I know, apo. I heard the water. Hold out your hands.
From the aparador she lifts something wrapped in black cloth. Through the cloth, it smokes. Her fingers redden where they touch it, and she sets her jaw against it.

lola_watch.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_watch.text: It was your Lolo's. Then it was mine to keep, not to use. It has not wanted me for a long time.
Her hands shake. The cloth slides. The watch drops toward the floorboards.

qte.lesson: It's falling. Watch the big ring close on the white circle. When it glows green, press SPACE (A button) or TAP.

miss.banner: It hits the boards. A hairline crack across the crystal.

lola_watch.text: He catches it a hand's width from the boards. It does not burn him. It is warm, like something asleep.

It hits the boards with a crack that should have split the case. The case is fine. Across the crystal runs a hairline crack, thin as a hair. Teo picks it up. It does not burn him. It is warm, like something asleep.
On the wall downstairs, all nine stopped clocks tick once, together, and stop again at 4:17.

lola_watch.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_watch.text: ...So. It knows whose turn it is.

lola_watch.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_watch.text: Later. You have a man downstairs who is forgetting his own name. Bring the oil from the altar, and the knife you think I don't know about.

berto_turns.text: The viewing room is cold. The water on the tiles has spread to the walls. Aling Nena sleeps through all of it, and so do the cousins on the bench.
Mang Berto stands over his own coffin. He is not reading the ribbons any more. His jaw has come unhinged, a little, and keeps opening.

berto_turns.speaker: Mang Berto
berto_turns.text: The cushion... the... what was in the cushion, iho? I had it a minute ago.

berto_turns.speaker: Mang Berto
berto_turns.text: Whose job... whose... I'm so hungry, iho.
Lola throws the bottle of langis from the stairs, end over end, across the room.

miss.banner: It shatters. You coat the blade from the floor and cut your palm: -8 HP

berto_turns.text: Coconut oil, blessed every Friday at the Quiapo altar. Teo runs it down the blade of his balisong, and the steel steams.
Glass on tile. Teo drags the blade through the spilled oil on the floor and opens his palm on a shard doing it. The steel steams anyway.

berto_turns.speaker: Lola Ising
berto_turns.text: You don't hurt them, apo. You hurt what's eating them. Cut the hunger out, and he'll remember.

berto_turns.speaker: Teo
berto_turns.text: A balisong and a bottle of oil. Walang atrasan, Teo. No backing out.

hatid.text: The darkness tears off Mang Berto like a wet coat and drains away between the floor tiles. What is left is a tired man in a driver's cap.

hatid.speaker: Lola Ising
hatid.text: Now send him. His whole name, and that his fare is paid. Say it like you mean it.

hatid.speaker: Teo
hatid.text: Ernesto Calma. Your fare is paid. Go home.

Somewhere there is no river, a ship's horn sounds. A lantern swings in the doorway of the parlor, on the prow of a narrow boat no one else can see. The ferrywoman Magwayen does not get off. She never does.

hatid.speaker: Teo
hatid.text: The cushion. Twelve thousand. You weren't drinking it.

hatid.speaker: Mang Berto
hatid.text: So it was your job after all.
He steps onto the boat. The lantern goes out. The water on the tiles is only water, and then it is not even that.

hatid.speaker: Lola Ising
hatid.text: Since you were four. You told me about the woman on the stairwell landing. I told you it was a dream, because I wanted it to be.

lola_answers.text: They sit on the stairs, the way they did when Teo was small and a wake ran late.

lola_answers.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_answers.text: I'll answer you one thing tonight. Only one. Choose well, apo, because tomorrow I'm on a bus.

remember.what: you asked why she was leaving

lola_answers.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_answers.text: We are sundô, Teo. Your Lolo, his mother, her father. We walk the dead home before something hungrier finds them first.

lola_answers.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_answers.text: The watch is cut from the heart of a balete, the tree where Sidapa marks how long each of us will live. It can borrow time from that tree. A second. A minute. A flood.

lola_answers.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_answers.text: And every second it borrows, it writes down. Against this family. Someone always comes to collect.

lola_answers.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_answers.text: Because people are coming for that watch, and I would rather they followed an old woman to Vigan than knocked on a door with you behind it.

lola_answers.speaker: Teo
lola_answers.text: One seat. You bought one seat.

lola_answers.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_answers.text: The watch was supposed to go to the Salonga family in Tondo tonight. Old sundô, older than us. Then it ticked for you. So now I don't know what I'm doing. That's the truth. Are you happy?

lola_answers.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_answers.text: Your Lolo borrowed four minutes and seventeen seconds, once, to push a flood out of this street. It cost him ten years. He died at sixty-one, looking eighty.

lola_answers.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_answers.text: Those clocks downstairs stopped at the moment he finished. I never wound them again. I didn't want to hear them count.

lola_answers.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_answers.text: Keep it on you. Against your skin. And Teo: never point it at anyone you love.

lola_answers.speaker: Lola Ising
lola_answers.text: Because it will tell you the truth.

act1_hook.text: 2:03 AM. Lola Ising is asleep in her chair at the top of the stairs, glasses on, rosary in her lap.

act1_hook.speaker: Teo
act1_hook.text: Never point it at anyone you love. She said it like a dare. She knows me.
Teo opens the watch. He turns it toward her.
The hands spin, slow, and settle. Not on the time now. On a time.

two_forty.text: 2:05 AM. Teo shakes Lola awake. She listens to all of it with her glasses pushed up on her forehead.

two_forty.speaker: Lola Ising
two_forty.text: Everyone has a time, apo. I'm seventy-five. Mine was never going to be a surprise.

two_forty.speaker: Teo
two_forty.text: It's thirty-five minutes away, 'La! It's not a time, it's a reason. Something is coming here, at 2:40.

two_forty.speaker: Teo
two_forty.text: So I stay. I sit at the bottom of these stairs with the balisong until it's 2:41, and then we argue about it.

two_forty.speaker: Lola Ising
two_forty.text: If it's coming here, I want you out of this house.

two_forty.speaker: Lola Ising
two_forty.text: ...You have your Lolo's temper. Then use it. Go to the water. That's where it starts, always. Find it before it finds the door. Come back before the bells.

two_forty.speaker: Teo
two_forty.text: Mang Berto's underpass. The child in the water. The rust.

two_forty.speaker: Lola Ising
two_forty.text: One more thing. The old way, before you leave. Salt on the threshold, or the door open so you can hear me call?

two_forty.speaker: Teo
two_forty.text: Salt keeps things out. An open door lets her call me.

options: Lay the salt line, like she taught me
Leave the door open, so I hear her

two_forty.text: A line of rock salt across the threshold, from the jar by the altar. Lola watches him do it and says nothing, which means he did it right.
Teo props the door with a chair. Lola says nothing, which means she would have chosen the salt.

estero.text: The estero behind Evangelista Street. A concrete creek with a tin roof of squatter houses over it. No rain tonight, and the water is up to the second rung of every ladder.
At the end of the creek, where it meets the underpass, a new pumping station hums behind a chain-link fence. On the fence, a logo: a rising sun in a circle. HIRAYA ENERGY. LIWANAG PARA SA LAHAT.

estero.speaker: Teo
estero.text: Light for everyone. At two in the morning, pumping a creek that shouldn't be full.
The watch ticks faster against his ribs as he walks toward the fence, like a heartbeat climbing stairs.

estero.speaker: Teo
estero.text: Rust. The whole creek smells of it. Same as Mang Berto's pillow.

estero.speaker: Teo
estero.text: A man in a Hiraya jacket paid Mang Berto to drive him here at midnight. Now I'm here at two.
Three ways in: a hole in the fence by the pump house, the crying under the bridge, and a rusted catwalk over the water.

options: Through the fence to the pump house
Down to the crying under the bridge
Along the catwalk, over the water

estero.text: Inside the fence: cables as thick as Teo's arm run from the pump down into the creek, and the creek water around them glows a faint, sick blue.

estero.speaker: Teo
estero.text: They're not pumping water out. They're pumping something out of the water.
Under the bridge, the crying stops the moment his shoes touch the bank. A baby's blanket floats past, empty, and folds itself under like a hand closing.

estero.speaker: Teo
estero.text: Mang Berto stopped for a crying baby. That's how it got him. Nobody in Quiapo drives past a crying baby.
From the catwalk, Teo can see shapes under the water. People. Lying on the bottom of the creek in rows, eyes open, waiting. None of them are breathing. None of them need to.

estero.speaker: Teo
estero.text: The unsent. Every drowned soul in this creek that never got a hatid. Someone's keeping them here.
All three ways end at the same place: the pump house fence. And between Teo and the fence, three people who are awake at two in the morning for reasons of their own.

hub2_tess.text: A woman in a duster sits on the steps of the nearest house over the creek, awake, as if she has been awake for weeks.

hub2_tess.speaker: Aling Tess
hub2_tess.text: You're looking at the water. Everybody looks at the water now. Three weeks ago nobody looked at it.

hub2_tess.speaker: Aling Tess
hub2_tess.text: My Bong went in after a ball. Nine years old. The Hiraya guards pulled me back from the fence. They said he drowned. They never let me see the water. They never gave me a body to bury.

hub2_tess.speaker: Teo
hub2_tess.text: No body. No wake. No hatid. He's down there with the others.

hub2_tess.speaker: Aling Tess
hub2_tess.text: If you're from the church, tell Father I still light the candle. Every night. Tell him I don't know where to point it.
Teo does not say he is not from the church.

hub2_celso.text: At the bridge, a barangay tanod in a reflective vest is drinking gin out of a coffee cup and pretending it is coffee.

hub2_celso.speaker: Tanod Celso
hub2_celso.text: Curfew, boy. Unless you're a Dimaculangan. Are you a Dimaculangan? You have the face. Pido's face.

hub2_celso.speaker: Teo
hub2_celso.text: Everybody over sixty on this side of Quiapo says that. Nobody under sixty knows what it means.

hub2_celso.speaker: Tanod Celso
hub2_celso.text: Hiraya pays our electric, pays our tanod allowance, paid for the new basketball court. Kapitan Obet signed the permit for that pump himself. Free light for everybody, he said. Who says no to light?

hub2_celso.speaker: Tanod Celso
hub2_celso.text: Kapitan Obet. Three weeks ago. Same week the kid went in. Coincidence, ha? Everything is a coincidence in this barangay.

hub2_guard.text: At the fence, a Hiraya security guard, maybe nineteen, holds his flashlight like it might protect him from something.

hub2_guard.speaker: Hiraya guard
hub2_guard.text: Sir, bawal po. Restricted. I'm just contractual, sir, please.

hub2_guard.speaker: Teo
hub2_guard.text: What do they pump out of that creek?

hub2_guard.speaker: Hiraya guard
hub2_guard.text: I don't know, sir. I don't ask. A white van comes at two every night, from the Wellness Center in Taguig, and takes the tanks. I sign the sheet. That's all.
He glances at the pump house. Then at the watch chain hanging from Teo's pocket, ticking loud enough to hear. Then he turns his flashlight off and walks the other way, which is a kind of answer.

creek_rises.text: 2:18. Teo reaches the pump house fence. The watch in his pocket is ticking so hard he can feel it in his teeth.
The creek feels it too. The surface bulges. Faces press up against it from underneath, the way they pressed up through the floor of the parlor in 1998.

creek_rises.speaker: Teo
creek_rises.text: Same as Lolo. Same as the old story. Except I don't have a sundang. I have a balisong and Lola's oil.
Among the faces, a small one. A boy of nine with his mouth open, reaching up for a ball that is not there.
They come up out of the water all at once, hungry, and the watch is the warmest thing they have felt in years.

options: Hold your ground on the bank
Get your back to the fence

creek_rises.speaker: Teo
creek_rises.text: Walang atrasan. Not one step back from the water.

creek_rises.speaker: Teo
creek_rises.text: Fence at my back. They come at me from the front or not at all.

dead_sundo.text: Inside the pump house, a folding chair. In the chair, an old man with a black panyo around his left wrist. He has been dead for less than an hour.

dead_sundo.speaker: Teo
dead_sundo.text: A panyo on the left wrist. Like Lolo in the old photographs. He's a sundô.
His ID, clipped to his shirt: AMBROSIO SALONGA, 47. The face on the ID is a man of forty-seven. The face in the chair is a man of ninety.

dead_sundo.speaker: Teo
dead_sundo.text: Salonga. The family in Tondo. Lola's plan. The watch was supposed to go to him tonight.

dead_sundo.speaker: Teo
dead_sundo.text: Salonga. Lola sends a Christmas card to Tondo every year.
On his lap, a ledger: names and dates in five different hands, back to 1901, every one a soul sent home. The last line is in fresh ink, the pen still in his fingers.
Around his neck, a string of balete beads, the kind his family would have used the way Teo's used a watch. Every bead is cracked through.

dead_sundo.speaker: Teo
dead_sundo.text: He borrowed until there was nothing left to borrow. That's what it looks like. That's what it looks like when they collect.

dead_sundo.speaker: Teo
dead_sundo.text: 2:22. I could send him. It takes a minute I might not have.

options: Take the ledger and keep moving

dead_sundo.speaker: Teo
dead_sundo.text: Ambrosio Salonga. Your fare is paid. Go home.
For a moment the old man in the chair is forty-seven again, and his eyes open, and they are not afraid.

dead_sundo.speaker: Mang Ambo
dead_sundo.text: It wasn't the Hiraya men, Dimaculangan. It was what they feed. Run.
Teo tucks the ledger into his jacket. It is heavier than paper should be.
Outside, along the creek, the streetlights go out one by one, from the far end toward the pump house. The last one, right above the door, flickers. Then it goes too.

aswang_drop.text: Rusted iron screams overhead. Something heavy lands on the catwalk above the door, and the catwalk bends.
Too many joints. Skin like wet tar. A head that hangs upside down from its own neck, and at its ear, blinking green, a plastic clamp stamped with a little rising sun.

aswang_drop.speaker: Teo
aswang_drop.text: Diyos ko. It's tagged. Somebody tagged it like a cow.
It turns its upside-down face toward Teo, and then toward the watch in his fist, and it smiles.

aswang_drop.speaker: Teo
aswang_drop.text: A balisong, Lola's oil, and a watch I don't know how to use. Walang atrasan.

after_aswang.text: The aswang comes apart into oily smoke, and the smoke goes down into the creek, and the creek, for a second, glows blue all the way to the river.
Teo is on his knees at the water's edge. In the black water, his reflection looks back.
At his left temple, a streak of white hair that was not there an hour ago.

after_aswang.speaker: Teo
after_aswang.text: It turned back the moment that thing killed me. I felt it. Like falling up a staircase. And it wrote it down. It wrote it down against me.
On the water, small lights rise, one for every face that was under it, and drift downstream toward a lantern that waits where the creek meets the river. One of them is small, and it bobs like a ball.

after_aswang.speaker: Teo
after_aswang.text: Bong. Your fare is paid, little one. Go home. Your mother is lighting a candle.
On the water, small lights rise, one for every face that was under it, and drift downstream toward a lantern that waits where the creek meets the river.
On the catwalk, the tag that fell off the aswang's ear still blinks green.

options: Take it: evidence, even if it's tracking you

after_aswang.speaker: Teo
after_aswang.text: Green light, blinking against my palm. If it's telling someone where I am, let them come.
The tag dies with a small, offended chirp.

gate_ram.text: Headlights. An engine screaming down the service road straight at the chained gate, and Teo is between the gate and the creek.
The gate is about to come apart.

miss.banner: Thrown by the blast: Teo starts the next fight 10 HP down

gate_ram.text: An old electric-company bucket truck, the bucket still on its boom, the doors painted over in grey. At the wheel, in embalmer's coveralls: Kardo, fifty-three, who has prepared every body in Punerarya Dimaculangan for twenty-eight years.

gate_ram.speaker: Kardo
gate_ram.text: And before that I climbed poles for the electric company, and before that I watched your Lolo push a river uphill. Get in.
Down the service road, a white van with a rising sun on its side pulls away from the far end of the pumping station. No headlights. Something in the back is banging to get out.

gate_ram.speaker: Teo
gate_ram.text: 2:31. Lola's time is in nine minutes. The van is getting away.

remember.what: you chose Lola over the van

truck_talk.text: The bucket truck smells of diesel, formaldehyde and 3-in-1 coffee. Kardo drives like the road personally owes him money.

They chase the van four blocks along Quezon Boulevard, close enough for Teo to see the passenger window roll down. A woman's profile. A white streak at her temple, like his. Then the van turns under the Quiapo overpass and is simply gone.

truck_talk.speaker: Kardo
truck_talk.text: Lost it. Hiraya vans don't show up on anything. I'm turning back.

truck_talk.speaker: Kardo
truck_talk.text: Your Lola called me a little after two. Said you'd gone to the water with that watch. Said, Kardo, it's time.

truck_talk.speaker: Teo
truck_talk.text: Kardo is staring at my hair.

truck_talk.speaker: Kardo
truck_talk.text: Your Lolo asked me to stay near this family. So I learned to embalm, because you can't stay near a funeral parlor for twenty-eight years by accident. That's who I am. The one who stayed.

truck_talk.speaker: Kardo
truck_talk.text: I was the lineman who cut the power. I counted, kid. Two hundred and fifty-seven seconds. I've never been able to stop counting things since.

truck_talk.speaker: Kardo
truck_talk.text: Hiraya paid every electric bill on Hidalgo Street this year. Free power. You know what free power buys a company? Quiet. And a lot of creeks nobody asks about.

truck_talk.speaker: Kardo
truck_talk.text: That streak. That's from the watch.

truck_talk.speaker: Teo
truck_talk.text: It killed me. The aswang. And then it hadn't.

truck_talk.speaker: Kardo
truck_talk.text: Then listen to me, because your Lolo didn't listen to anybody. That watch doesn't give. It lends. Every time it saves you, somebody in your family pays.

parlor_taken.text: 2:41. Hidalgo Street. The truck brakes so hard the bucket swings. One minute late.
At the far end of the street, the tail lights of a second white van, no headlights, turning the corner onto Quezon Boulevard.
From inside it, through the metal, an old woman's voice shouts one word.
Then the corner, and the tail lights, and nothing.
The parlor's neon is dark. The door of Punerarya Dimaculangan stands open.
The salt line is unbroken. Whatever came for her could not cross it, so it did not try: it cut a hole through the wall beside the door, a perfect circle, the edges still hot.
And in the salt, written with a finger, in Lola's hand: HUWAG KANG SUSUNOD.  Don't follow.
On the step, one of Lola's slippers. The other is in the street.

Inside: Aling Nena and the cousins asleep in their chairs, too deeply, a sweet chemical smell in the air. Mang Berto's coffin knocked off its stand. The aparador upstairs torn open, and the boxes for Vigan emptied on the floor.
Teo opens the watch and points it at her empty chair.
The hands do not settle on a time. They do not move at all. Where her time was, the dial is blank.

morgue.text: The basement of Punerarya Dimaculangan: Kardo's embalming room. Steel table, formaldehyde, a radio, and a jeepney seat bolted to the wall for a couch.
Kardo puts a cup of 3-in-1 coffee into Teo's hands and closes his fingers around it, because they will not stop shaking.

morgue.speaker: Kardo
morgue.text: Drink. Sugar first. Then we think.

morgue.speaker: Teo
morgue.text: They took her. While I was out there fighting their pet. That's what it was for. To get me out of the house.

morgue.speaker: Kardo
morgue.text: Hand. Give it. You cut it on the glass? You're your Lolo's grandson, all right.

morgue.speaker: Kardo
morgue.text: Ribs. Don't argue. Your ribs are telling me you hit that gate with your face.

morgue.speaker: Teo
morgue.text: Kardo has the suture kit out.

options: "I'm fine. Tell me where she is."

morgue.text: Kardo stitches the way he embalms: fast, neat, no talking. It helps. Teo hates that it helps.

morgue.speaker: Kardo
morgue.text: I don't know yet. But I know who's going to tell us. Sit.

kardo_1998.speaker: Kardo
kardo_1998.text: You want to know about 1998? The real one. Not the one your Lola tells, and not the one your Lolo never told.
He tells it the way the player has already seen it: the knocking coffins, the drowned rising, the watch, the river pouring backward down Hidalgo Street. Two hundred and fifty-seven seconds.

kardo_1998.speaker: Kardo
kardo_1998.text: Then he went white, and I thought that was the price. That was not the price.

kardo_1998.speaker: Kardo
kardo_1998.text: The water had to go somewhere. It went to Santa Ana. All at once. Thirty-one people drowned there before sunrise, kid. Riverside families. One of them was a bus driver named Villacorta, and he had a son.
A long beat. The radio hisses between stations.

kardo_1998.speaker: Teo
kardo_1998.text: Lolo saved this street. He drowned another one.

kardo_1998.speaker: Kardo
kardo_1998.text: Maybe. He never said. He spent his last eleven years lighting candles in Santa Ana every third of June, and he never said.

kardo_1998.speaker: Kardo
kardo_1998.text: ...Yeah. I think he did. I think he knew where it was owed, and he chose us. I don't know if I'd have chosen different.

kardo_1998.speaker: Kardo
kardo_1998.text: That's what I said too, the first ten years.

tape.text: On a shelf behind the formaldehyde, a Nescafé can. Inside it, a cassette, labelled in Lola's careful capitals: KARDO. KUNG WALA NA AKO BAGO ANG KAMPANA.  If I'm gone before the bells.

tape.speaker: Kardo
tape.text: She gave me this in May. Made me swear not to play it unless I had to.
The tape recorder clicks. Hiss, and then a voice calm as a kettle on the stove.

tape.speaker: Lola Ising (tape)
tape.text: Teo. If Kardo is playing this, they came for me, and they came for the house, and you were not in it. Good. That was the plan.

tape.speaker: Lola Ising (tape)
tape.text: The bus to Vigan was for them to follow. One seat. I meant to be the one they chased. If you are hearing this, it did not work. Don't blame Kardo. Blame the old woman who thought she could outrun a ledger.

tape.speaker: Lola Ising (tape)
tape.text: You asked me about the watch. Here is the rest. It isn't a curse. It's a contract. Your Lolo signed it with a flood. I've spent twenty-eight years trying to make the payments small.

tape.speaker: Lola Ising (tape)
tape.text: You asked me why I was leaving. Now you know. I'm sorry I lied about the packing. I'm not sorry I tried.

tape.speaker: Lola Ising (tape)
tape.text: You asked me about your Lolo. He was a good man who did one terrible, necessary thing, and I never forgave him for it, and I loved him every day.

tape.speaker: Lola Ising (tape)
tape.text: Domeng will have told you about the candles. They are not for me, apo. They are for her. You'll understand.

tape.speaker: Lola Ising (tape)
tape.text: Every second you borrow, the watch writes down. Don't let them make you pay for our mistakes. And Teo: there is a place where the Pasig tastes of rust. Kardo knows it. That's where the door is.

tape.speaker: Teo
tape.text: Rust. Mang Berto's pillow. The creek. She knew where all of this was going.

options: Say nothing. Listen to the hiss.

tape.speaker: Lola Ising (tape)
tape.text: ...And if I know you, you just said you're coming. Then come carefully.
Under the hiss, very faintly, Lola is humming. The same song she hummed on the stairs when a wake ran late.
Kardo stops it without a word. The silence in the morgue sounds like the inside of a coffin.

the_offer.text: At 3:20 AM, Teo's phone rings. Unknown number. A soft voice, the kind that has never once had to shout.

the_offer.speaker: Atty. Benitez
the_offer.text: Mr. Dimaculangan. Attorney Lorna Benitez, Hiraya Energy, Legal. I'm sorry for the hour, and I'm sorry about your grandmother's door.

the_offer.speaker: Atty. Benitez
the_offer.text: Safe. The Hiraya Wellness Center in Taguig. Voluntary protective custody. Her heart is not what she tells you it is, Mr. Dimaculangan. Did you know she takes three different pills?

the_offer.speaker: Teo
the_offer.text: The Wellness Center. The guard at the fence said a white van comes from there every night at two, and takes the tanks.
A photo arrives. Lola Ising in a clean hospital bed, an IV in her arm, holding today's Inquirer under her chin. She looks absolutely furious, which means she is alive.

the_offer.speaker: Atty. Benitez
the_offer.text: Here is our offer. Hiraya has already acquired Kapitan Obet's paper on your building. We forgive it, all of it. We return your grandmother home, tonight. We pay you a fair price for the lot, if you want to sell, and a better one if you don't.

the_offer.speaker: Atty. Benitez
the_offer.text: And the other debt. The one written in that watch. We can carry it for you. We have resources that can pay what your family owes, so that you never go white at thirty.

the_offer.speaker: Teo
the_offer.text: Resources. You mean the people in that creek.

the_offer.speaker: Atty. Benitez
the_offer.text: I mean the thirty-one people who drowned in Santa Ana on 3 June 1998, Mr. Dimaculangan. Our chairman was seventeen. He held his father's hand on a roof until he couldn't. We are not asking you to stop protecting your street. We are asking your family to stop drowning ours.

the_offer.speaker: Teo
the_offer.text: And the worst part is she believes it. And the worst part is, so do I. A little.

the_offer.speaker: Teo
the_offer.text: Lola, the house, the debt. All of it, for the watch.

options: "I need proof she's all right. In person."

the_offer.speaker: Atty. Benitez
the_offer.text: I understand. I would have, too, at your age. We'll speak again.

the_offer.speaker: Atty. Benitez
the_offer.text: Of course. I'll arrange it. A car will come.

the_offer.speaker: Atty. Benitez
the_offer.text: Thank you. Stay where you are. We'll collect it.
The line goes dead. On the radio, between stations, something begins to tick.

hound_in.text: The street-level window grating over the morgue sink buckles inward, bolt by bolt.

hound_in.speaker: Kardo
hound_in.text: You kept the tag?! Of course they found us!

hound_in.speaker: Kardo
hound_in.text: They didn't need a tag. They've had this house on a map for twenty-eight years.

hound_in.speaker: Teo
hound_in.text: I said yes! I said yes, why are they breaking in?

hound_in.speaker: Kardo
hound_in.text: Because 'collect' doesn't mean the watch, kid. It means you.
Something long and white drops through the window onto the steel table: four piston legs, a ribbed body, and one round lens that glows like a rising sun.

hound_in.speaker: Kardo
hound_in.text: Finally. Something I'm qualified to fight.
Kardo pulls a coil of copper jumper wire off the wall, clamps one end to the steel table and the other to the morgue's breaker, and grins for the first time all night.

hound_in.speaker: Kardo
hound_in.text: I wire it, you cut it, I light it up. Don't stand in the water.

after_hound.text: The hound's lens cracks, sparks, and goes dark. Its ribbed chest splits open on the steel table.
Inside, where an engine should be: a glass vial of blue light, the same sick blue as the creek. And in the light, pressed against the glass, a face.
A woman Teo has never seen, maybe thirty, her mouth moving without sound. Someone else's mother. Someone else's unsent.
Mang Ambo Salonga. Forty-seven again. His mouth moving without sound.

after_hound.speaker: Kardo
after_hound.text: Ginhawa. Breath. They're bottling them, Teo. That's their green power. That's what's running Hidalgo Street's free electricity.
Kardo's hand, on the edge of the table, is shaking now too.

after_hound.speaker: Kardo
after_hound.text: If people saw this. If the whole barangay saw this, plugged into their electric fans...

after_hound.speaker: Teo
after_hound.text: Kardo wants proof. The soul in the glass wants out.

options: Break the vial and send them home
Keep it. People need to see this.

after_hound.speaker: Teo
after_hound.text: Your fare is paid. Go home.
The glass breaks in his hand without his hand closing. A lantern swings in the morgue doorway for half a second. Kardo looks at the empty table for a long time.

after_hound.speaker: Kardo
after_hound.text: ...That was the right thing. I'm going to be angry about it for a week.
Kardo wraps it in a clean towel like something newborn and puts it in the freezer between two unclaimed bodies.

after_hound.speaker: Kardo
after_hound.text: I'm sorry, whoever you are. We'll send you home. After everyone sees.
Teo's phone buzzes. A text from Aling Nena, at 3:51 AM: Nakita ko sa cushion. 12,000. Salamat, iho. Hindi pala siya umiinom. (Found it in the cushion. Thank you. He wasn't drinking after all.)

dawn.text: 5:40 AM. Upstairs, the parlor is waking up. The gas wears off the mourners one by one, and they find the room as the raiders left it.
Aling Nena is putting Mang Berto's flowers back in their stands with her own hands. Mang Domeng arrives with his first candles of the day and stops in the doorway.

dawn.speaker: Teo
dawn.text: They took her, Mang Domeng. In the night. While I was out.
Mang Domeng sets down his candles very carefully, the way you set down something you are afraid you will throw.
At the door: Kapitan Obet, in yesterday's barong, two tanods behind him, and a new folder.

dawn.speaker: Kapitan Obet
dawn.text: Teo. Iho. I heard. I'm sorry. I came to secure the property, that's all, there are papers...

dawn.speaker: Teo
dawn.text: You signed the permit for the pump on the estero, Kap. Three weeks ago. The same week a nine-year-old went in that water.

dawn.speaker: Kapitan Obet
dawn.text: ...It was a pumping station! For flooding! They said flooding!

dawn.speaker: Kapitan Obet
dawn.text: They bought the paper on this building, Teo. Three weeks ago. They paid me triple. I thought: Ising gets her money, everyone wins. Nobody said anything about taking her. I swear on my mother.

dawn.speaker: Teo
dawn.text: Three weeks ago. And last night you stood at Mang Berto's wake with a folder and told my Lola it was due Friday. You were collecting a debt you'd already sold, Kap.

dawn.speaker: Kapitan Obet
dawn.text: ...They asked me to keep the pressure on. So she'd sell. That's all. Pressure.

dawn.speaker: Kapitan Obet
dawn.text: And you threw me out of a wake, so don't look at me like that.

dawn.speaker: Kapitan Obet
dawn.text: You promised me Friday. I believed you. I'm the one who didn't keep his word. That's the truth.

dawn.speaker: Teo
dawn.text: Kapitan Obet sold us. He's also the only one here who's been inside Hiraya's offices.

options: "Then help me get her back. You owe her."
Say nothing. Let the room look at him.

remember.what: you threw him out of the house
you told him he owes her

dawn.text: He goes. The two tanods hesitate, then follow him, and one of them leaves his flashlight on the table for Teo, which nobody mentions.

dawn.speaker: Kapitan Obet
dawn.text: ...The Wellness Center. Fourth floor is the real one, not the clinic. I've been to the third. That's as high as they let a barangay captain go. I'll draw you the lobby.
Aling Nena looks at him. Mang Domeng looks at him. Every cousin who ever borrowed from his 5-6 looks at him. Kapitan Obet looks at the floor, and then he leaves the folder on the table and goes.

dawn.speaker: Mang Domeng
dawn.text: Your Lola paid me for forty days of candles, iho. I'm lighting the first one now. Not for her. For whoever brings her home.

photo.text: Upstairs, Teo kneels in what is left of Lola's room. Among the things the raiders threw out of the aparador: a photograph in a plastic sleeve. He has never seen it.
Lola Ising, young, on the stairs of this parlor, the walls still dark with flood water. In her arms, a baby girl.
On the back, in Lolo Pido's handwriting: LIWAYWAY. 3 HUNYO 1998. SIYA ANG SUSUNOD.

photo.speaker: Teo
photo.text: Liwayway. Mama's first baby. She drowned in the flood. Mama still calls from Dubai on her birthday and doesn't say why.

photo.speaker: Teo
photo.text: 'She is the next.' The next what? She drowned, Mang Kardo. Didn't she?
Kardo has followed him up the stairs. He looks at the photo, and then over the banister at the stopped clocks on the parlor wall below, all reading 4:17, and then at the floor.

photo.speaker: Kardo
photo.text: ...Ask your Lola. When we get her back.

photo.speaker: Teo
photo.text: You were there. You were on those stairs.

photo.speaker: Kardo
photo.text: I was there. And I promised her. Ask me anything else.

photo.speaker: Teo
photo.text: He knows. He's known for twenty-eight years.

photo.speaker: Kardo
photo.text: Somebody knocked on this door on the morning after the flood, Teo. That's all you get. That's already more than I should.

photo.speaker: Kardo
photo.text: ...Thank you. Get two hours of sleep, downstairs, where it's quiet. Then Taguig.

cliffhanger.text: 6:17 AM. The morgue is quiet. Kardo is asleep on the jeepney seat with the suture kit still open on his chest. Upstairs, the stopped clocks still say 4:17.

cliffhanger.speaker: Teo
cliffhanger.text: Never point it at anyone you love.

cliffhanger.speaker: Teo
cliffhanger.text: She never said anything about pointing it at myself.
Teo opens the watch and turns it toward his own face.
The hands do not settle on a time. The dial turns, and turns, and shows a date: the night the moon goes dark. Laho. Forty-seven days from now.
On the radio, the morning news replays last night's press conference from BGC: Hiraya Energy announces LIWANAG, free power for every household in Metro Manila, starting the night of the eclipse.

cliffhanger.speaker: Gregorio Villacorta
cliffhanger.text: My father drowned when I was seventeen, in a flood no one could explain. I have spent my life making sure no Filipino family will ever again be at the mercy of things they cannot see.
The TV in the corner, sound off, runs the same replay, with LAST NIGHT in the corner of the screen. Beside Gregorio Villacorta, in a white suit, stands his daughter and chief operating officer.
Teo knows her profile. He saw it a few hours ago, in the window of a van with no headlights, on its way back from the creek.
Celeste Villacorta. Twenty-eight. When she tucks her hair behind her ear for the cameras, there is a streak of white at her left temple. Exactly where Teo's is.
